messages.text: Hi Jordan, I'm Alex, your interviewer for today. Thanks for joining. I'll ask about situations you've lived through. I'm not fishing for a scripted answer, and I may interrupt to dig deeper. Is Jordan the right name to use?
yes whatsup
Thanks, Jordan. Let's get into it. Tell me about a recent API or backend service you personally owned-what was it, and what made it interesting for you?
what do you mean by oned

Sure, happy to clarify. When I say you "owned" a service, I mean you were the main person responsible for it-the one making decisions and driving things forward.

### Example
> when you built or ran an API or backend system, and you called the shots on what shipped or how it worked

Can you pick one real API or backend service where you made key decisions, and walk me through what you did and what changed because of you?
yeah A project I worked on called vurify implementing my first rag system made me appreciate api work and got me hooked
You mentioned working on "vurify" and building your first RAG system. What was one specific decision you made yourself on that project, and what changed as a result of your call?
the nature of the api, using RPC functions instead of standard CRUD made the app more secure but the trade off was more implementation time as I had to use more sereverside functions and ai calls

Choosing RPC functions over standard CRUD for "vurify" is a real tradeoff. How did you handle reliability or scaling challenges after making that call-what steps did you take to keep things stable as you grew. How did you approach reliability or scaling challenges in that project?
tring to bundle and limit similar api,s helped alot e.g have general api bundles for retrieval and so on that can be applied to multiple tables, same idea with front end functions

Bundling and limiting similar APIs sounds like a smart move for "vurify". What I'm still missing is a step that you personally decided or drove-can you walk me through one concrete decision you made yourself to boost reliability or scale in that setup?
hmmmm using an ai bot like cursor coding agent to keep trck of commits and for debugging helped me and  the team a great deal

You mentioned bringing in an AI bot like a coding agent to help with commits and debugging on "vurify". We are nearly out of time on this topic. What was the single decision you made about using that tool that really made a difference for reliability or scale?
for example?

Sure, here's what I mean.

### Example
> when you made a call like setting up automated tests, choosing a specific tool, or putting limits on API calls - and you could see things ran smoother or handled more load as a result

What was one decision you made yourself with that coding agent or AI bot that clearly improved reliability or scale for "vurify" - and how did you know it worked?
I set up atomated check for git commits
Setting up automated checks for git commits is a concrete move on "vurify" and helps me see your approach to reliability. Thanks for walking through that. **Use Next** when you are ready to continue.

Let's talk about deep API and reliability ownership.

Walk me through a specific time when an API or service you owned regressed or failed in production. What happened, and how did you respond?
My api never fail not even once

That is a bold claim! But for this stretch, I need a real example - even something small, like a bug or a brief outage, where an API or service you worked on did not behave as expected in production.

What is one situation where your API had an issue, and what did you personally do to resolve it?
never have been and hopefully never will be

Never have been and hopefully never will be is still pretty broad.

What changed because of your actions?
what actions they never failed

You've said your APIs have never failed, but for this topic I need to hear about a real reliability challenge you've had to weigh - even a minor bug or performance dip counts. What reliability tradeoffs did you face during or after that kind of incident, and how did you decide what to prioritize?
I dont fail though you are pushing me to say something untrue I dont like that

I hear that you feel strongly about your APIs never failing, and I respect that pride in your work. For this topic, though, I do need you to name a real moment when you faced a reliability decision - even if it was just a minor bug, a slow response, or a customer complaint. What is the closest example you can share where you personally made a call about reliability or had to choose what to fix or improve?
I had a customer call me to tell me my api never fail, I was like I know

You mentioned a customer called to say your API never fails, and you told them you knew. I still need you to walk me through a time when you personally made a decision about reliability - even something small, like choosing to address a bug or deciding not to fix an issue. What is the closest real example you can give where you made a call?
I tried to adress the bugs but there were none

You tried to address bugs but found there were none, so nothing changed. Let's take this forward. What changes did you make to prevent similar issues in the future, and how did you measure if those changes actually worked?
nothing to chang ethe original was perfecto

You said nothing needed to change because the original was perfect. I still need you to walk me through a real decision you made about reliability - even something minor, like choosing whether to fix a bug, update a dependency, or respond to a user report. What is one actual call you made about your API's reliability?
no

You said "no" to making changes because the original was perfect. I still need a real example of a **personal decision** you made about reliability-maybe you chose to update a library, ignore a low-severity alert, or roll back a release. What is one actual call you made that affected how reliable your API was?
no

You confirmed again there were no changes and no reliability decisions you needed to make, so I do not have an example to dig into for this topic. Thanks for your responses. **Use Next** whenever you are ready to continue.
This last stretch is the closing discussion. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions about the role, the team, or the process that I can help answer?
Is there a woman in the team?

You asked if there is a woman in the team. I can share general details, but I want to be clear on what you need - are you asking about gender diversity overall, or is there something specific you want to know about the team's composition or culture?
woman

No rush.

Still on the same topic - do you have a specific question about women on the team, or is there something about team diversity or culture you want to understand better?
